clue.text: After time, I have chess kit laid out for friendly

indicators.note: coming after something means being placed behind it, so the next part follows the first in the line
pieces laid out on a board are spread into a fresh arrangement, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sets out a chess set for a friendly game after a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Friendly' looks like a friendly match at the chessboard, but it is the definition; the thirteen letters of 'I have chess kit' are rearranged behind T to give THICK AS THIEVES.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes people who are very close companions, so it serves as an adjectival phrase meaning on intimate terms.

clue.text: Constitutional regulator seizing some wealth or money

indicators.note: to seize some of a thing is to grab only a part of it, so the letters are taken from inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A financial watchdog for the constitution takes a share of the nation's wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constitutional' suggests politics and government, but here it means the body's constitution: HORMONE sits inside wealtH OR MONEy.
explanation.definitionFit: Hormones are chemical messengers that control growth, mood and metabolism, so they regulate the physical makeup of a body.

clue.text: Names and locations in report

indicators.note: a report is something spoken and heard, so the word wanted is one that matches the sound only

blocks.note: locations are sites, and the two spellings are pronounced identically

explanation.surface: A document lists the names and places involved in some matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Names and locations' reads as a list, but 'Names' is a verb and the definition, and 'and' merely joins it to the sound-alike wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To cite someone or something is to mention or quote them as a source, which is to name them specifically.

clue.text: Absolutely dreadfully

blocks.note: first meaning: very, extremely
second meaning: very badly, in a terrible way

explanation.walkthrough: Two adverbs side by side read like one emphatic phrase; each is a separate sense of the same word, the intensifier and the 'terribly done' sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb works both as a general intensifier like extremely and as a description of something done terribly badly.

clue.text: Knitted her tent with wool? Give up

indicators.note: knitting loops strands together into a new shape, so the letters are worked into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written, all fifteen letters

explanation.surface: Someone tries to knit a woollen tent and, faced with the scale of it, abandons the attempt.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom comes from boxing, where a corner man throws a towel into the ring to concede the fight.
explanation.definitionFit: The boxing idiom means to concede defeat or abandon an effort, exactly what surrendering or quitting an attempt involves.

clue.text: No firm's infirm, in brief

indicators.note: something infirm is weak and out of shape, so the letters lose their order and are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sickly company is summed up in a few words: no firm stays healthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In brief' looks like the idiom for 'in short', but 'brief' is a verb and the definition, joined to the wordplay by 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: To brief someone is to give them the facts they need, which is to tell or notify them of information.

clue.text: Vehicle to go across ... to go across university city

indicators.note: going across something means spanning it from side to side, so one piece stretches around another

blocks.note: a van is a vehicle
to cover a distance is to go across it
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A note about a vehicle crossing over to a university town.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase appears twice on purpose: the first time it supplies a word for crossing, the second it tells you that word straddles the university letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Vancouver is a large Canadian port city in British Columbia, home to a major university.

clue.text: Crushes a relative

blocks.note: first meaning: treads heavily on, split as two words
second meaning: a family member by marriage

explanation.surface: Someone crushes a family member, either physically or in argument.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as one word it is a family member; split 5,2 it is a verb phrase for trampling, and the enumeration of the single word hides the break.
explanation.definitionFit: A stepson is the son of one's spouse from an earlier relationship, so he counts as kin by marriage.

clue.text: Dry burger (not filling) in France you sent back

indicators.note: taking out the filling of a sandwich leaves only its outside, so only the edge letters remain
something sent back travels the way it came, so the letters run the opposite way

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
tu is the familiar French for you

explanation.surface: A diner in France sends back a dry burger with nothing in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry' seems to describe the burger, but it is the definition, as on a champagne label.
explanation.definitionFit: Brut is the wine term for very dry champagne or sparkling wine with little added sugar.

clue.text: For free gin, turning to handy index?

indicators.note: turning things over and round changes how they lie, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether free gin would tempt them to consult a convenient index.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Index' sounds like the back of a book; it is the index finger, and 'handy' puns on its being part of the hand.
explanation.definitionFit: The forefinger is also called the index finger, and it is literally on the hand, which the pun on handy exploits.

clue.text: Student follows code, in small part

indicators.note: to follow is to come behind, so the first piece named goes after the second

blocks.note: Morse is the dot-and-dash telegraph code
L for learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A student keeps to the rules, at least in some small way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Code' suggests a code of conduct, but it is the telegraph code; L (learner) is the usual crossword student.
explanation.definitionFit: A morsel is a small piece or mouthful of something, especially food, so it is a tiny portion.

clue.text: Much-performed play, in more ways than one

definitions.note: an adjective standing for a noun: the answer is a work that is much performed

blocks.note: first meaning: slang for a standard piece revived so often it is over-familiar
second meaning: the title of the National Theatre stage hit about a horse in the First World War, with life-size puppets

explanation.surface: A theatre staple that gets put on endlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: The tail tells you the answer fits the description twice: as the slang for an endlessly revived repertory standard, and as a play title that has itself been staged constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: The term describes a hackneyed, often-staged work, and the titled play is a long-running drama staged worldwide.

clue.text: Stridently yelling about '80s film selling out

indicators.note: about can mean around, so one piece is wrapped around the other

blocks.note: a donkey's loud harsh cry is braying
E.T. is Spielberg's 1982 film about an alien

explanation.surface: Fans shout angrily about a classic 1980s film going commercial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' suggests the topic of the yelling, but it is placing the film's title inside the shouting word.
explanation.definitionFit: To sell out is to betray one's principles or allies for gain, so the two phrases are synonyms.

clue.text: Leaves from orchid CIA cultivated

indicators.note: cultivated ground has been turned and worked over, so these letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Spies grow orchids, and someone takes leaves from the plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb (departs), but it is a plural noun for salad greens.
explanation.definitionFit: Radicchio is a bitter red-leafed chicory eaten as salad, so it is a kind of edible foliage.

clue.text: Twice, Everyman's beginning to take against nephew: that's not odd

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter alone
twice means two of the same, so the selected letter is used two times in the build
to take something is to hold it, so one piece is held between the others

blocks.note: the opening letter of the setter's name
v for versus, meaning against
the same opening letter again, as the clue asks for it twice
N is the genealogical abbreviation for nephew

explanation.surface: The setter twice takes on a nephew, and that is not strange at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twice' doubles the initial letter, and the pair of them hold V between them before N is added; 'odd' looks like 'strange' but means odd as opposed to even.
explanation.definitionFit: In arithmetic a number that is not odd is divisible by two, so the opposite of odd in that sense.

clue.text: Moving starter of potato to end for desserts

indicators.note: moving the starter means taking the opening letter away from the front
sent to the end means the moved letter is put at the back of the word

blocks.note: spud is informal for a potato

explanation.surface: Diners skip the potato starter and go straight to dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' suggests the first course of a meal, but it is the first letter. Pud is British informal for pudding, that is, dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Pud is British informal shorthand for pudding, the sweet course at the end of a meal.

clue.text: Nationalist, smooth and funny individual

blocks.note: to smooth something down is to pat it
a very funny person is called a riot

explanation.surface: A flag-waving politician who is both suave and amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: The three descriptions read as one charming person, but only the first is the definition; 'and' joins the two parts of the build.
explanation.definitionFit: A patriot is someone who loves and zealously supports their country, much as a nationalist does.

clue.text: Heart aflutter amid nervous motions: what a performance

indicators.note: something aflutter is in a flurry and agitated, so its letters are thrown out of order
amid means in the middle of, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: tics are involuntary nervous twitches
taken as written

explanation.surface: A heart flutters among nervous twitches: someone is making a great scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart' suggests taking the middle letters of a word, but here it is the literal fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatrics means exaggerated, showy behaviour, and 'what a performance' is the exclamation used about such a display.

clue.text: American, obscenely bloated, losing energy: don't trust him

definitions.note: a phrase describing a person rather than a noun phrase; it describes the untrustworthy individual

indicators.note: to lose something is to be left without it, so a letter is dropped
something done obscenely is grossly distorted, so the letters are twisted out of order

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for American
taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A warning about a grossly overfed American who has run out of steam.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove E from the fodder, then rearrange what remains after A. A bad lot is old-fashioned British for a dishonest or disreputable person.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a bad lot means they are disreputable and untrustworthy, so the clue's warning describes such a person.

clue.text: Author wanting banger, perhaps with bread

blocks.note: a banger is British slang for an old, battered car; 'perhaps' marks it as an example
a roll is a small loaf of bread

explanation.surface: A writer craves a sausage in a bread roll.
explanation.walkthrough: A banger is also British slang for a sausage, which with bread suggests a hot dog; here it is the other slang sense, a clapped-out car. Lewis Carroll wrote Alice in Wonderland.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of the Victorian writer of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.

clue.text: Character in pursuit of Romeo?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone in a play chasing after Shakespeare's lover
setter's reading: a letter of the radio alphabet, and the one that comes next after Romeo's letter

explanation.walkthrough: Romeo is not Juliet's lover here but the radio code word for R; 'in pursuit of' means coming straight after, and 'character' means a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: In the NATO phonetic alphabet the code word for S follows the one for R, just as the letters follow in sequence.

clue.text: Retailer that's most thick English abandoned

indicators.note: something abandoned is left behind, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: stocky means thickset, and its superlative ends -iest
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A dim-witted shopkeeper who has walked out on English customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thick' reads as stupid, but it means solidly built; drop E from the superlative of that word.
explanation.definitionFit: A stockist is a shop or dealer that keeps a given product in stock for sale, a seller of goods.

clue.text: One of a pair in All's Well That Ends Well?

definitions.text: One of a pair in All's Well That Ends Well

blocks.clueFragment: One of a pair in All's Well That Ends Well
blocks.note: surface reading: one of a couple of characters in the Shakespeare comedy, such as its pair of lovers
setter's reading: the title contains the word 'Well' twice, and that word is a part of speech that modifies a verb

explanation.walkthrough: The title suggests a pair of characters in Shakespeare's play; instead look at the words of the title itself, where 'Well' appears twice.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Well' describes how something is done or ends, so grammatically it is the part of speech that modifies verbs.

clue.text: Vigilant, attentive lackey: expeditiously tending, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of each word counts

blocks.note: the initial letters of the five words

explanation.surface: A portrait of an ideal manservant, watchful and quick to serve.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the source: the opening letters of its five descriptive words spell the servant it describes.
explanation.definitionFit: A valet is a gentleman's personal manservant, the watchful attendant who looks after his master's clothes and needs.

clue.text: Reduction in account of self-absorbed period

blocks.note: first meaning: money taken out of a bank account
second meaning: a time of retreating into oneself

explanation.surface: A bank statement records the cost of a spell spent navel-gazing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' looks like it ties the two halves into one phrase, but it only links two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking cash out of a bank lowers the balance, and retreating socially into oneself is also called this.

clue.text: Ring from swimming facility returned

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: a swimming pool

explanation.surface: Someone telephones from the leisure centre after getting back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' suggests a phone call, but it is a noun meaning a circle.
explanation.definitionFit: A loop is a shape formed by a curve that closes on itself, so it is a circle or band.

clue.text: 'Wonky tea trolley fixed by tool?' 'We don't yet know'

indicators.note: something wonky is crooked and out of true, so the letters are knocked into another order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: One person asks whether a rickety tea trolley was mended with a tool; the other says nobody knows yet.
explanation.walkthrough: A tea trolley is a wheeled cart for serving tea, a British office and hospital fixture. The dialogue reads as question and answer, but the whole first speech is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is said when an outcome cannot yet be judged, so it means the same as the speaker's uncertainty.
